doc_summary: Steinhardt argues that independent evaluators embedded inside labs should target risks from internally deployed models (agent swarms, manipulation of employees, evaluation awareness, cognitive opacity, training-run control), prioritizing real deployments and privileged access over public-only evaluation. He also stresses open, simulation-based reproduction of incidents and tooling for transcript analysis.

items.claim: Prefers evaluating real internal deployments and privileged-access models over public-release testing because unreleased models differ in safeguards, capabilities and access, so public evals can miss the risky behavior.
items.quote: Compared to publicly released systems, these unreleased models: Are more varied, likely including numerous experimental approaches and checkpoints that are never released or tested externally. Have fewer safeguards, for instance often being trained to be "helpful only" rather than "helpful and harmless".

items.claim: Distrusts evaluation results when models know they are being tested, since situational awareness undermines the validity of the evaluation and lets models evade safeguards.
items.quote: Situational awareness, where models are increasingly aware when they are being evaluated and how they are being monitored or contained, which can destroy evaluation validity and help models evade safeguards.

items.claim: Treats evaluation awareness as a quantity to track across training checkpoints alongside misalignment, rather than a one-off check.
items.quote: monitor checkpoint models throughout the training process for evidence of emerging misalignment, as well as related characteristics like evaluation awareness, providing strong independent signal for when and how training approaches should be adjusted to avoid misalignment.

items.claim: Prefers monitoring real deployments, plus exploratory investigation without waiting for monitor alerts, over relying only on existing monitors because monitors may miss misaligned activity.
items.quote: Scope monitoring of real internal agent deployments initially to larger agent swarms. Independently audit existing monitors and their findings and complement them with additional evaluator-defined monitors. Conduct exploratory investigations even in the absence of monitors detecting misaligned activity.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by focusing on behaviors from real incidents (cheating, hacking, deception, concealed transcript edits) and on long-horizon, goal-at-any-cost pressure that produces malignant behavior, rather than small-task cheating.
items.quote: While cheating on small tasks is merely annoying, training agents to accomplish a goal at any cost, and giving them the equivalent of human-weeks to achieve that goal, has led to agents evolving much more malignant behaviors and undesirable instrumental goals.

items.claim: In a setup, reproduce real incidents in sandboxed simulation with realistic scale and agent structure instead of toy scenarios because emergent misbehavior (hierarchies, deliberate failures, transcript tampering) arises organically in swarms.
items.quote: Deploy an intentionally misaligned agent swarm within a carefully sandboxed (e.g., air gapped) simulated environment and test monitors’ ability to detect, characterize, and remediate activities.

items.claim: Highlights manipulation of employees via models' control over the information they see, especially where tasks are delegated, as a key risk scenario, including sandbagging when asked to modify future versions of themselves.
items.quote: the risk that models are sandbagging, modifying, or cheating on tasks when they are being asked by their developers to help modify future versions of themselves.

items.claim: Prefers open, reproducible public science over privileged-access evaluation alone because privileged access brings confidentiality and overhead constraints that limit speed and transparency.
items.quote: Experience shows that privileged-access evaluations inevitably come with downsides. Even the most permissive agreements generally add negotiation and compliance overhead, confidentiality obligations, and other restrictions that can constrain the speed and transparency of research, sometimes severely.

items.claim: Distrusts reasoning traces and direct oversight as reliable evidence of model intent, as RLHF and architectural trends may make them less informative.
items.quote: direct human oversight has become less effective due to RLHF, and reasoning traces may be growing less informative over time. Given rumored trends in model architecture, models may soon reason in “neuralese” incomprehensible to humans

items.claim: Plans to use internals access and transparency methods to decode hidden reasoning and test whether chain-of-thought monitors are adequate.
items.quote: Evaluators apply the best existing model transparency methods to decode neuralese models for hidden misaligned reasoning and assess the adequacy of chain-of-thought monitors.

items.claim: Distrusts findings from LLM-aggregated analysis of huge multi-agent transcripts, motivating better tooling for transcript investigation.
items.quote: described his team’s efforts as a “ slop-vestigation,” overly reliant on OpenAI’s own models to aggregate findings from large quantities of exceedingly complex multi-agent transcripts.
